arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Muldrow's counsel argued that a sex-based transfer violates Title VII regardless of tangible harm.
The City's counsel argued that the statute requires proof of injury to the employee.
Justices questioned whether the word against implies a requirement for tangible harm.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: Jatonya Muldrow claims the City of St. Louis transferred her due to her sex. She argues this violates Title VII. The City argues the transfer caused no tangible harm. The Court must define the legal standard for such claims.

paragraphs: Muldrow wants the Court to rule that a sex-based transfer violates Title VII without proof of tangible harm.
The City wants the Court to require proof that a transfer caused tangible harm to constitute discrimination.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Muldrow argues that forcing a transfer based on sex is discrimination under Title VII regardless of the job's relative quality.
The City argues that the word against requires proof that the treatment injured the employee.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines the scope of workplace anti-discrimination protections. It determines whether employees must prove tangible harm to sue over biased transfers. The outcome shapes employer liability for personnel decisions. It clarifies the meaning of the statutory phrase discriminate against. It affects how courts evaluate claims of sex-based employment actions.
